1.pericope_label: The second journey urged, and Judah made surety

schools.summary: Gill notes that the famine grew sorer in Canaan and that this is recorded to explain the second journey, that Judah spoke because Reuben had been refused, Simeon was held in Egypt and Levi stood out of favour over Shechem, and that Judah besides had an interest with his father and authority among his brethren; he adopts Calvin's account of how the household was fed while insisting some corn must have been left for the women and children. Calvin asks how so small a purchase could have supported three hundred people, rejects the guess that the servants had been sold, and supposes the servants lived on acorns, herbs and roots as the whole region must have done; he suspects Judah of overstating the case to extort what his father would never freely grant, allows that unrecorded exchanges may have passed and even that Joseph may have served a formal summons, and reads the long disputation as showing how hard Jacob found the parting, since he contended for Benjamin as though striving for the salvation of his whole family. Calvin also makes the famine a trial of the promise, the lord of the land being denied bread in it as a stranger.

Henry finds Jacob in the character of a good master of a family, careful to provide food convenient, and reads the request for a little food as fitted to a time of scarcity, when a little must suffice and nature is content with a little; in Judah's suretyship he sees the evidence of a real repentance, since Judah's conscience had lately smitten him for what was done to Joseph, and being unable to restore that brother he makes what amends the case admits by doubling his care of this one.

Clarke objects that the word rendered lad is not the one used of a child and would be better given as the youth or the young man, Benjamin being at least twenty-four and by some accounts thirty and having a family of his own; he renders the pledge literally, that Judah should sin against his father all his days, and lays out the plea from self-preservation as a chain, since without Benjamin there is no journey, without the journey no corn, and without corn Benjamin perishes with the rest. Wesley reads the suretyship, with Henry, as the evidence of a repentance made good by doubled care.

Keil and Delitzsch explain that Judah conducted the negotiation because Reuben had already been refused and Levi had forfeited his father's confidence through his treachery to the Shechemites, and observe that Joseph had never asked directly after their father and their brother but had forced the account out of them by the charge of spying, so that Judah's report of the interview was a fair one. Ellicott puts Benjamin between twenty and thirty, takes the word lad in Judah's mouth for a term of affection that suits the age, and disposes of the claim that he is drawn as a mere boy by pointing out that Rebekah and Shechem are called the same thing in Hebrew; he finds Judah's pledge more manly and so more persuasive than Reuben's offer of his children's lives, and no slight matter, since it meant standing before his father for life as a guilty man.

debates: Why Judah rather than another made the plea. Gill and Keil and Delitzsch both clear the ground by elimination, Reuben having been refused, Simeon held in Egypt, and Levi discredited by Shechem; Gill adds Judah's own standing and readiness of speech; Ellicott brings out the same preference by contrasting his pledge with Reuben's.

How Jacob's household lived through the famine. Calvin argues that the corn bought could only have fed Jacob's own line, the servants subsisting on acorns, herbs and roots like the rest of the country; Gill takes the explanation over but insists that a remainder of corn must have been kept, and that Canaan yielded a little of its own.

How old Benjamin was and what the word lad implies. Clarke rests on the choice of the Hebrew term and gives an age of at least twenty-four; Ellicott sets the range between twenty and thirty and answers the objection from parallel uses of the same word.
outliers: Calvin's conjecture that Joseph may have had a legal summons served, citing his brother to appear as in a judicial cause.
Calvin's reading of the famine as a trial of the promise itself, the appointed lord of the land being denied bread in it as a stranger.
Ellicott's comparison of Judah's pledge with Reuben's earlier offer to pledge the lives of his own children.
themes: a surety in place of restitution

11.pericope_label: Jacob yields, and sends a present with a prayer

schools.summary: Calvin observes that the fruits sent were for the most part not precious, the condition of holy Jacob being not such that he could send a royal present, and that fruits are not always valued at their cost; he takes the prayer for a pattern of how to act when perplexed, omitting nothing expedient while relying on God, since the tranquillity of faith has no affinity with indolence and nothing is to be ascribed to our own industry when every means has been tried; he notes that Jacob treats the hearts of men as subject to God, whom we too seldom acknowledge as their secret governor; and on the closing words he canvasses several senses, inclining to plain resignation and comparing Esther's if I perish, I perish, while suspecting that Jacob spoke so chiefly to work upon his sons and make them careful of their brother. Gill takes the money to have been doubled because scarcity had made corn doubly dear, and keeps it distinct from the restored sum as a third parcel.

Henry admires Jacob's persuasibleness, that he would be ruled by reason though his inferiors urged it, and having once refused to let Benjamin go allowed himself to be over-persuaded; from which he draws that it is no fault but our wisdom and duty to alter a resolution when there is good reason, constancy being a virtue where obstinacy is not, and unchangeable resolve being God's prerogative. He finds prudence and justice in three provisions: the money sent back with the charitable construction that it was an oversight, which he makes a rule of restitution, since to keep what comes by another's mistake once the mistake is known is to keep it by deceit; the doubled money against a risen price or a ransom for Simeon; and a present chosen from what Canaan exported and Egypt lacked.

Clarke makes the doubled money the returned sum together with the price of a fresh load, and admits that the present defeats precision, since after all the labour of commentators we must be content with probabilities and the almonds are perhaps the only article known with certainty, Canaan producing the best in the east; he canvasses resin for the balm, grape syrup or common honey for the honey, gum storax, an ointment of myrrh, and pistachios or dates or walnuts for the nuts. On the closing words he stands alone, rendering the verse as a prediction and holding that God gave Jacob at that moment a supernatural assurance that his children would be restored. Wesley repeats Henry's judgment on the altering of a resolution.

Keil and Delitzsch prefer second money, a further sum rather than a doubling, and read the closing words as resigned submission to the will of God. Ellicott reports both renderings of the money and finds the second confirmed by the phrase used later in the chapter; he identifies the honey as grape-honey boiled down to a third of its bulk, still exported from Hebron into Egypt by the camel load, and the nuts as pistachios, which will not grow in Egypt; he infers from the gift both that Canaan still yielded some vegetation, without which Jacob could not have kept his cattle alive, and that the smallness of the present argues a scarcity even of fruit rather than any simple notion of Egyptian greatness; and he reads the last clause as pious resignation joined with heartfelt anguish, the supplied words of my children only lessening its pathos.

debates: What the doubled money was. Gill makes it a doubling forced by the dearness of corn and a parcel distinct from the money restored; Clarke makes it the restored money plus the price of a new load; Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott read it as second money, a further sum, Ellicott appealing to the wording later in the chapter.

What the present consisted of. Clarke lists the competing identifications and concedes that only the almonds are certain; Ellicott decides for grape-honey and pistachios on grounds of trade and cultivation; Calvin declines the question and rests on the modesty of the gift.

Whether the closing words are resignation or prediction. Ellicott, Keil and Delitzsch and Calvin all hear submission, Calvin adding a motive of working upon the sons; Clarke alone renders the verse as a prophecy and supposes a supernatural assurance given to Jacob at that moment.
outliers: Clarke's admission that after all the labour of commentators the list of gifts remains conjecture, the almonds excepted.
Ellicott's note that the grape-honey of Hebron was still going into Egypt by the camel load in his own day.
Calvin's rule that the tranquillity of faith has no affinity with indolence, so that reliance on God and diligence in means belong together.
themes: a resolution altered for good reason
a present of what the land had left
if I be bereaved, I am bereaved

15.pericope_label: Brought into the house, and met by the steward

schools.summary: Calvin traces the brothers' panic to conscience, since without the judgment of God tormenting them there was no cause to apprehend such perfidy, and offers the innocent construction that the governor may only have wished to show his friends the unwonted spectacle of eleven brothers at one table; he argues that the steward was in Joseph's confidence, both because he ascribes the money to the particular God of their father rather than to any god of Canaan, which an Egyptian would not have done unless taught better, and because Simeon had been kept gently rather than as a suspected spy; he makes the steward's confession the credit of his master, who could not correct the public superstition but maintained the worship of the one God within his own walls; and having weighed the dinner hour and the sending of each man's portion from the host's table, he breaks off because such things are trivial and not conducive to piety. Gill observes that buyers of corn were lodged at an inn in the city and not in the governor's house, so that the summons was irregular in itself.

Henry notices that Joseph would not leave off selling corn even to greet Benjamin, nor trust the work to another, since employment must take place of civility in its season; he finds the brothers making the worst of everything, as the guilty and timorous will, and expecting to be charged as cheats who had used the hurry of the market to carry off corn unpaid for; he judges that the steward was not in the secret, arguing from the later scene in which no one was suffered to be present when Joseph made himself known; and he draws from the steward's answer that of what we get by deceit we cannot say God gives it us, so that the words both acquit the brothers and silence further enquiry.

Clarke reads the order for dinner as the Hebrew idiom slay a slaying, a great slaughter got ready for a great entertainment; he says a guilty conscience needs no accuser, gives the brothers' phrase its force from wrestling, where a man rolls himself upon a fallen antagonist to keep him down, and notes that the asses they feared to lose were no small part of the family's wealth; he guesses the steward was himself a Hebrew, not at liberty to reveal the matter but able to promise a happy issue. Wesley draws with Henry the lesson that what is got by deceit cannot be said to be given by God.

Ellicott answers the standing objection that the narrator errs because the higher Egyptians and especially the priests ate no flesh, pointing to representations of feasts from this period showing animal food in abundance, to animals sacred in one district being freely eaten in another, and to a priestly rule that barred mutton, pork and fish rather than beef and goose; Keil and Delitzsch note that the imperative in the order for dinner stands in its older form. Ellicott observes that the brothers would not enter the house until they had assurance, leaves open whether the steward was instructed for the occasion or belonged to a household generally trained in his master's religion, glosses the word for treasure as what we should call a windfall, and distinguishes the travelling bags in which the silver lay from the corn sacks, remarking that only one brother found his money at the halt and that the point is their being a full day out before anything was noticed.

debates: Whether the steward was in Joseph's confidence. Henry says he was not, arguing from the privacy Joseph later required when he disclosed himself; Calvin says he was, on the double ground of his naming the God of their father and of Simeon's gentle usage in prison; Clarke supposes him a Hebrew who knew everything and was not free to tell it; Ellicott leaves both possibilities standing.

Why the brothers took the invitation for a trap. Henry has them expecting a charge of carrying off unpaid corn; Clarke lays it to a guilty conscience that needs no accuser; Calvin to the judgment of God tormenting them, and adds that a wholly innocent motive for the invitation was available had they been able to see it.

Where the steward's knowledge of the God of the Hebrews came from. Henry and Wesley credit his master's instruction; Calvin makes it evidence that Joseph kept the true worship alive inside his own house at some risk; Clarke supposes the man a Hebrew by birth; Ellicott allows either a briefing for the occasion or a household trained in general.
outliers: Ellicott's rebuttal of the charge that the meal is an anachronism because Egyptians of rank ate no flesh.
Clarke's derivation of the brothers' phrase from wrestling, where the victor rolls himself upon the man he has thrown.
Calvin's suggestion that the governor may have wanted nothing more than to show his friends eleven brothers at one table.
Calvin's refusal to dwell on the customs of the meal, as trivial and not conducive to piety.
themes: a summons that felt like a trap
a guilty conscience needs no accuser
a steward who knew more than he said
your God and the God of your father

26.pericope_label: Dinner with Joseph, and Benjamin preferred

schools.summary: Gill observes that by calling their father Joseph's servant the brothers made him do obeisance through them, so that the sun of the second dream stooped as well, and takes Benjamin's fivefold portion for a test of whether the others would resent him. Calvin reads the separate tables as a lesson on pride, since a nation that separates itself from others must itself be pure while superstition carries its impurity within and despises everyone else; rather than suppose the Egyptians held their own governor polluted he conjectures that Joseph sat apart to maintain his dignity; and he notes that Joseph meant to remain unknown but that affection broke out beyond the purpose of his mind, defending the merriment at table as honourable liberality rather than intemperance, so that drunkards may not plead the example of the holy fathers.

Henry watches the dreams come true by degrees as the brothers bow with their present and again with their news, and thinks the form thy servant our father was one Jacob had taught them; he finds the enquiry after Jacob fit for any old man, since we are dying daily and it is strange we are yet alive; he defends the tears as no disparagement to great and wise men while noting that Joseph withdrew to shed them, gracious weepers not proclaiming their tears; he sets the three tables down to hospitality, to a generous unwillingness to impose Hebrew company on Egyptians, and to the early distance between Jew and Gentile; he rejects the notion that the brothers seated themselves by custom, since their wonder would not then have been recorded; and he takes the fivefold portion for a trial of whether they would envy Benjamin as they had once envied Joseph his finer coat, adding that no one should be pressed to eat or drink to excess.

Clarke turns the greeting to Benjamin into a complaint about language, since the words were the ordinary address of an elder to a younger in the east, emphatic once but reduced in his own day to phrases that mean just nothing, and used even in David's time as a cloak, as when Joab kissed Amasa and stabbed him; on the separate tables he adds two causes of his own, that the Hebrews were shepherds and Egypt had been ruined by the shepherd kings, and that the Hebrews killed and ate animals the Egyptians held sacred. Wesley is content to note that the brothers' cares were over and they ate their bread with joy.

Keil and Delitzsch hear real feeling in the address my son, which they call paternal and fitted to Benjamin's youth, reckoning him sixteen years younger than Joseph and an infant when Joseph was sold; they explain the separate tables by the Egyptian spirit of caste, which barred Joseph from eating with his inferiors and those inferiors from eating with foreigners, citing the Greek whose knife no Egyptian would touch; and they say the seating by age forced on the brothers the idea that this great man had been supernaturally enlightened about their family. Ellicott calls the obeisance the literal fulfilment of the dream of eleven sheaves and finds a fitness in corn-buyers figured as sheaves, makes Benjamin a child of eight or nine at the selling and nearly thirty now so that Joseph's question is one of pure surprise, observes that the word abomination proves the scruple religious and not merely social, holds that the brothers must have credited Joseph with divination since precedence is a serious matter in the east, and thinks the fivefold portion more probably dictated by simple love than by any design to test them.

debates: How old Benjamin was at the two ends of the story. Keil and Delitzsch make him sixteen years younger than Joseph and an infant at the selling; Ellicott makes him a child of eight or nine then and nearly thirty at this meal, and builds Joseph's surprise upon the contrast.

Why Egyptians and Hebrews could not eat together. Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both appeal to caste and to the Greek knife, Ellicott insisting from the word abomination that the ground was religious; Clarke adds the national memory of the shepherd kings and the eating of sacred animals; Calvin looks past the causes to the pride the custom expressed, and reassigns Joseph's separate table to rank rather than pollution.

What the fivefold portion was for. Gill and Henry read it as a deliberate trial of the brothers' old envy; Ellicott thinks it more probably nothing but affection; Calvin comes near the same, treating it as love breaking out beyond Joseph's intention to stay unknown.
outliers: Clarke's complaint that an eastern blessing once full of meaning had decayed into forms of words that mean just nothing, with Joab's kiss as the extreme case.
Henry's rule that tears of tenderness are no disparagement even to great men, but that gracious weepers should not proclaim them.
Calvin's argument that whoever separates himself from others on religious grounds must himself be pure, so that superstition claims the privilege in vain.
themes: seated by an age no stranger knew
